questions.solution: Correct Option A - Conn syndrome: The most likely diagnosis in this patient is primary hyperaldosteronism (PHA), also known as Conn syndrome. PHA is a common cause of secondary hypertension, characterized by the excessive production of aldosterone by the adrenal gland, leading to salt retention and potassium loss. The typical clinical presentation of PHA includes hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis, which can lead to muscle weakness, fatigue, and headaches. The elevated PAC level confirms the diagnosis of PHA, and the presence of an adrenal nodule on the CT scan suggests an adenoma as the cause of the excess aldosterone secretion. The diagnosis can be further confirmed by performing a saline infusion test or a captopril challenge test. Incorrect Options: Option B - Cushing syndrome: Cushing syndrome is a rare disorder characterized by the excess production of cortisol by the adrenal gland, leading to hypertension, weight gain, glucose intolerance, and muscle weakness. However, this patient's presentation is not consistent with Cushing syndrome, as she has low serum potassium levels, which are not typically seen in this condition. Option C - Pheochromocytoma: Pheochromocytoma is a rare tumour of the adrenal gland that produces excess catecholamines, leading to hypertension, headaches, palpitations, and sweating. However, this patient does not have the classic symptoms of pheochromocytoma, and her low serum potassium level suggests a different diagnosis. Option D - Familial hyperaldosteronism: Familial hyperaldosteronism types I and II are rare genetic disorders that result in early-onset hypertension and hyperaldosteronism. Familial hyperaldosteronism type I is caused by mutations in the KCNJ5 gene, while type II is caused by mutations in the CACNA1H, CACNA1D, or CACNA1S genes. However, these conditions typically present at a younger age than the patient in this scenario. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Oral contraceptive pills: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is a genetic condition marked by impaired steroid hormone synthesis in the adrenal glands. As a result, there is an increase in the production of androgens and the accumulation of their precursors, which can cause female virilization. Most commonly, glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids are used in hormone replacement therapy to treat CAH by replacing the missing hormones. Though some CAH patients may still experience elevated androgen levels and hyperandrogenism-related symptoms, like excessive hair growth, irregular menses, even with adequate hormone replacement, this is not always the case. The best course of action in this situation for the patient's symptoms would be oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) secretion from the pituitary gland. OCPs contain estrogen and progesterone, which can inhibit the hypothalamic release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) and the pituitary gland's subsequent release of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). This may lead to a reduction in ovarian androgen production as well as a reduction in peripheral androgen activation. OCPs can therefore successfully lower androgen levels and ameliorate the symptoms of hyperandrogenism in females with CAH. It is not frequently used as a first-line treatment for CAH, despite the fact that it can be used to treat the symptoms of hyperandrogenism in conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Option C - Ketoconazole: Ketoconazole, an antifungal drug that can also inhibit steroidogenesis, is not frequently used to treat CAH because it has potentially harmful side effects. questions.solution: Correct Option D - Ptosis: The most likely cause of isolated oculomotor nerve palsy in a patient with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus is diabetic mononeuropathy , which occurs as a result of microangiopathic ischemia . Ptosis occurs in patients with CN III palsy because the levator palpebrae superioris muscle is innervated by the oculomotor nerve . Whereas patients with CN III palsy due to compression usually show dilated pupils , those with diabetic mononeuropathy normally do not have pupillary involvement because the microangiopathy typically involves the vasa nervorum within the oculomotor nerve , while the pial blood vessels (which supply the superficial parasympathetic fibres) are usually spared. CN III palsy due to diabetic or hypertensive microangiopathy usually improves with blood pressure and glycemic control . Patients should be monitored closely (every 2 days) during the first week. If the diplopia , ptosis , and/or external ophthalmoplegia worsen during this period or persist after 3 months, an MRI should be performed. questions.solution: Correct Option D - MRI with contrast: This patient is suspected of having prolactinoma given her history of secondary amenorrhea, negative pregnancy test, and elevated prolactin levels (> 200 ng/mL). Prolactin-secreting tumours of the pituitary gland are called prolactinomas. It is the most common secretory tumour of the pituitary gland. Prolactinomas arise from the monoclonal expansion of pituitary lactotrophs that have undergone somatic mutation. Based on the size of the tumours, prolactinomas can be classified as micro prolactinoma (smaller than 10 mm), macroprolactinoma (larger than 10 mm), or giant prolactinoma (larger than 4 cm) Prolactin levels are usually directly proportionate to the size of the tumour, ranging from below 200 ng/ml with less than 1 cm, 200 ng/ml to 1000 ng/ml with 1 cm to 2 cm, and more than 1000 ng/ml with tumour size more than 2 cm in diameter. A detailed history and physical examination are required to rule out the reversible causes of hyperprolactinemia, i.e. pregnancy, hypothyroidism, and medications. MRI with gadolinium is the preferred imaging modality for evaluating hyperprolactinemia as it best describes the anatomy of the hypothalamic-pituitary area. Incorrect Options: Option A - CT scan with contrast: It is not the most appropriate test to visualize the pituitary adenoma as the anatomy of the hypothalamic-pituitary area is not visible. Option B - Biopsy of the adenoma: It is not used for diagnosing prolactinoma because it is an invasive procedure with no added advantage over other tests. Option C - MR venography: MR venography is used to diagnose the conditions involving the cerebral veins, i.e. idiopathic intracranial hypertension and cerebral venous thrombosis secondary to a hypercoagulable state. @Neet_pg_bot
